steps.text: You found the pawn that two white pieces attack. This is how a **threat** begins: a move your opponent could play next that would win material or give checkmate. Black to move. Step through what happens if Black ignores it.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's queen and bishop both aim at the pawn on f7.

line.say: Black develops a knight and does not notice what White is aiming at.
The queen takes f7. The bishop protects her and the king has nowhere to go: checkmate.

claims.statement: If Black ignores the threat, the queen takes f7 with checkmate.

steps.caption: The same position. What if Black adds a second defender of f7?

line.say: The knight now also defends f7, so a capture there can be answered by the knight.

claims.statement: After the knight move, two black pieces defend f7.
Two white pieces still attack f7.

steps.title: The same attack, one defender more
steps.prompt: Black's knight went to h6, not f6. Predict first: does Qxf7 still win for White?

steps.text: A threat is only worth what it would gain. Znosko-Borovsky observed that a threat can pay off even if carrying it out would gain nothing, because the opponent must spend a move answering it. [H] Real threats against beginners usually do gain material, so treat every threat as real until you have checked.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's pawn has just reached e5 and attacks the knight on f6.

line.say: Black develops and ignores the pawn.
The pawn takes the knight.
Black recaptures, but has traded a knight for a pawn.

claims.statement: If Black ignores the pawn, White comes out ahead.
The knight on f6 is defended, so it is not loose.

steps.text: Notice that the knight was defended and still in trouble. Count what each side gives and takes in the exchange. When the attacker is worth less than the target, a defender does not save you; when it is worth the same or more, a defender usually does. Values are a rule of thumb: pawn 1, knight 3. Next, see how to answer the threat by moving away.

There are five answers to a threat. **Move away** the piece in danger. **Defend** it. **Capture** the attacker. **Block** the line between them. **Counter-attack** with a bigger threat of your own. List them all, then pick the one that leaves nothing else attacked. [I] The safest answer is usually the one that changes least.

steps.caption: The knight needs a square that no white piece attacks. Two of its squares are covered by the queen. White can chase the knight next move, but nothing is lost.

line.say: The knight steps to d5. No white piece attacks it there, so the threat is gone.

claims.statement: No white piece attacks d5.
The white queen attacks h5.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's pawn on b5 has just attacked the bishop on a4.

line.say: The bishop retreats to a square the pawn cannot reach and keeps its diagonal.

claims.statement: Before the move, the bishop on a4 is loose.
No black piece attacks b3.

steps.caption: Same position. This time White does nothing about it and plays a quiet pawn move.

line.say: White makes a quiet move and leaves the bishop where it is.
The pawn takes the bishop. White has lost a bishop for a pawn at most.

claims.statement: If White passes, the pawn wins the bishop.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black's king is on the back rank (the eighth row), boxed in by its own pawns. White's rook looks down the open file.

line.say: Black makes an unrelated move.
The rook reaches the back rank. The pawns block the king and the black rook cannot take: checkmate.

claims.statement: If Black passes, the rook reaches d8 with checkmate.

steps.caption: Now suppose Black had first moved a pawn one square forward. White to move.

line.say: The rook gives check on the back rank, as before.
This time the king has a square to escape to, so the threat is over.

claims.statement: The rook check is not checkmate.

steps.text: Second question: which of my own pieces is **loose**, attacked and not defended? A loose piece is the easiest thing for an opponent to win. In the next board the bishop on e4 is loose. Step through it and see Black's mistake.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white knight attacks the bishop on e4, and nothing defends the bishop.

line.say: Black plays a pawn move and does not notice the loose bishop.
The knight takes the bishop for free.

claims.statement: The bishop on e4 is the only loose black piece.
If Black passes, the knight wins the bishop.

steps.caption: Black to move. The knight on f3 attacks the pawn on e5, but the knight on c6 defends it.

line.say: Black adds a second defender and opens the bishop's diagonal. The pawn on e5 is now safe twice over.

claims.statement: One white piece attacks e5.
One black piece defends e5.
No black piece is loose.

steps.text: A useful picture: every piece of yours has a number of attackers and a number of defenders. In this course, loose means attacked and undefended. Many players use the word for any undefended piece, attacked or not. If the attacker is worth less than the target, even a defended piece can be in trouble. Now find the loose piece in a new position.

Before you play a move, imagine it already made and ask what your opponent can now take. Three leaks: **1.** the moved piece lands on an attacked square. **2.** the moved piece was guarding something. **3.** the move ignores a threat already there. The next boards show the first two.

steps.caption: Black to move, thinking of the knight to b4. The pawn on a3 attacks that square.

line.say: The knight lands on a square the pawn attacks.
The pawn takes the knight. Black has lost a piece for a pawn at most.

claims.statement: The a3 pawn attacks b4.
The move loses a piece.

steps.caption: Same position. Now the knight retreats to b8. Is anything left behind? It loses the e5 pawn and more (engine: about -2.5 at depth 16).

line.say: The knight steps back and no longer defends the pawn on e5.
The white knight takes the pawn, which now has no defender.

claims.statement: Before the move, one black piece defends e5.
After the move, nothing defends e5.
The retreat loses the e5 pawn and more.

steps.caption: Same position. A third idea: the bishop to b4, hoping to pin the knight on c3.

line.say: The bishop lands on b4, again a square the a3 pawn attacks.
The pawn takes the bishop. A pin means nothing if the pinning piece is lost.

claims.statement: The a3 pawn attacks b4.

steps.text: Often there is nothing to fix. Nimzowitsch, in My System, argued against the idea that every move must threaten or parry; quiet moves that improve a piece have value too. [H] Beginners may over-worry after every move. The two questions are quick: once the answer is no, follow your plan.

steps.caption: Black to move. No piece is loose and nothing White can play wins material by force; Ng5 is an idea to watch, since it would aim a second piece at f7.

line.say: The bishop develops to a good diagonal, eyeing f2. Nothing is left attacked.

claims.statement: No black piece is loose.
No white piece is loose.
This developing move is close to the engine's best.

steps.text: Your routine before every move: **1.** What does the last move threaten? **2.** Which of my pieces are loose? **3.** After my move, what can be taken? Capablanca names, in the notes to his own games, a time he missed an opponent's threat entirely. [I] The check is for everyone.

**Say it back.** Before I move, I ask what my opponent's last move threatens and whether any of my pieces is loose. If something is threatened I list my answers: move away, defend, capture the attacker, block, counter-attack. Then I imagine my own move and check what it leaves attacked. If nothing is threatened and nothing is loose, I carry on with my plan. After a game, I mark one moment where I was unsure.

steps.prompt: Optional, after your next game: mark one move where you were unsure. What did you think your opponent would do there? You will compare your answer with what the game shows.
